Today's quests

Part 1 · What Social Science is
01A day already made of systemsSocial Science in everyday life35 XP

Think about a day in your life. Nothing in it arrived on its own. Tap each part of the morning and follow the chain of people and decisions standing behind it.

—

You wake up in a house built with materials sourced from different places. The food you eat may come from various regions of the country. Before it reaches your plate, it has been harvested, processed, transported, bought, and sold through the efforts of many people. You travel on roads planned and maintained by public authorities. You study in a school shaped by educational policies and programmes. The electricity that you use is generated at distant power stations and delivered through a vast and complex network.

Even the simplest daily activities rely on systems of governance, economic production, social cooperation, and the natural environment. Human beings live in societies and depend on each other in many ways, and understanding these connections is the foundation of Social Science.

Pause and ponder
Pick one object within arm's reach right now. How many different people had to do something before it could sit where it is? You will not reach the end of the list.
02What kind of subject is this?Society, not the natural world25 XP

In Grades 6 to 8 you met Social Science through stories of people, places and events. Now it is worth saying plainly what it is. Mark each statement.

In simple words, Social Science is the systematic study of human society. It not only tells us what happened or where things are located, but also explains why events occur, how people live together, how environments influence life, how governments function, how economies operate, and how the past and the present together shape the world.

While subjects like Physics, Chemistry and Biology study the natural world, Social Science focuses on society, institutions, cultures and human interactions. Our lives are shaped by the environment, the institutions that govern us, the economic activities that meet our needs, and the traditions and ideas passed down through generations.

03A change in your localityLet's analyse · the method, in order25 XP

The chapter asks you to observe your surroundings and identify a change of the past five years — in transport, housing, education, technology or the environment. Put the steps of that enquiry in the order the book sets out.

Questions like why do some people live in crowded cities while others live in scattered villages? or why are certain regions more prone to floods? show that society does not function by chance. It is shaped by history, geography, institutions, resources and human choices.

Social Science helps us explore such questions and seek answers through careful observation, evidence and logical reasoning. Simple observations like these help you see society as one connected story rather than a collection of separate pieces.

Part 2 · Society through time and traditions
04From camp to cityHow society got to be the way it is35 XP

Society has not always been as it is today. Drag through thousands of years and watch what each new ability adds — and what it forces people to organise.

Early human communities depended directly on nature for survival. With time, people learnt to grow crops, domesticate animals, build settlements, develop tools, exchange goods, and organise systems of governance. Villages developed into towns, and towns grew into cities. New ideas, inventions and cultural exchanges gradually transformed ways of life.

To understand the present, we must trace this long journey of continuity and change — how societies evolved, how institutions developed, and how relationships between people and the environment transformed.

05India's knowledge traditionsEnquiry with deep roots30 XP

The effort to understand society through observation, reasoning and reflection is not new, and it did not begin in Europe. Match each idea or text to what it says.

Tap an idea, then tap what it means.

Early thinkers valued discussion, questioning and logical reasoning. The concept of the Pañchamahābhūtas describes the natural world as an interconnected system in which human life is embedded, helping explain how the environment influences settlement patterns, occupations, architecture, food habits and health practices. The idea of vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam — the world is one family — expresses the interconnectedness of human societies across regions and cultures.

Early reflections on governance in India linked political authority with public welfare and ethical responsibility. The Arthaśhāstra, attributed to Kauṭilya and composed about 2,300 years ago, examined administration, economic management, taxation, and the duties of rulers toward their people. Systematic thinking about governance and the economy existed long before modern academic disciplines developed.

A word to know
Pañchamahābhūtas — the five great elements of Indian philosophical traditions: earth (Pṛithvī), water (Āpaḥ), fire (Agni), air (Vāyu) and space (Ākāśha). Scholars used the idea to explain natural processes, the human body, and the relationship between living beings and the environment. Expressed in philosophical terms, it is an early attempt to understand nature as an interconnected system.
06How a social scientist finds outEvidence, not opinion25 XP

Modern Social Science continues an old legacy with new tools. Pick every method that actually belongs to it.

Social scientists observe people's lives, conduct interviews and surveys, examine documents, and compare different times and places. By gathering information from multiple sources, they develop explanations that are supported by evidence.

This way, Social Science explains both what endures and what changes, showing how the past shapes the present and how today's actions will influence the future.

Part 3 · Four lenses on one world
07One drought, five kinds of damageWhy one subject is never enough30 XP

The rains fail over one district. Tap each consequence and watch how far a single event travels beyond the field it started in.

—

Human society is complex, and no single field of study can fully explain it. A drought affects crops (environment), farmers' incomes (economy), government relief measures (politics), migration to cities (society), and traditional ways of coping with scarcity (culture).

To understand such situations, we must examine society from different perspectives. Social Science is therefore not a single subject but a group of related disciplines, each focusing on a different aspect of human life. Together, they help us understand society in a comprehensive and connected way.

08Which discipline asks this?The four core disciplines, and the wider family30 XP

Each discipline asks different questions, yet all are interconnected. Match each one to the question it is built to answer.

Tap a discipline, then tap its question.

In Grades 9–10, Social Science primarily draws from four core disciplines — Geography, History, Political Science and Economics — that together provide a comprehensive understanding of society.

Other disciplines such as Sociology, Philosophy, Anthropology and Psychology also form part of the broader Social Science family. These fields explore social relationships, ethical reasoning and human behaviour in greater depth, and will be developed further in higher grades.

09Geography · one place, five toolsWhere things are, and why there35 XP

Here is a single district beside a river. Switch the instrument and the same place answers a different question each time.

—

Geography studies the location and distribution of places, objects, materials and people, as well as the relationships between human societies and their surroundings. It seeks to understand where things are located, why they are found there, and how places — near or distant — affect one another over time.

It views the world as a system of interdependencies, integrating spatial perspectives (location and its significance) with temporal perspectives (change over time). Drawing on both natural sciences and social sciences, Geography helps answer questions like why India has historically been a hub of global interaction, and how the Indian peninsula's long coastline made contact with Africa, Europe and Southeast Asia possible.

10History · sorting the evidenceFour kinds of source35 XP

History writing draws on a wide range of sources. Each of these is pictured in your textbook. Sort every one into the kind of source it is.

History is the study of the human past, through which societies seek to understand people's experiences, values and changes over time. One of the oldest traditions of preserving cultural memory in Bharat is the itihāsa-purāṇa tradition, which through stories not only shares historical information but gives cultural meaning to events and people.

Modern historiography increasingly relies on empirical evidence, using human genetics, carbon-14 dating, archaeology and other scientific methods to establish timelines. Literary sources include travelogues, memoirs, correspondence, genealogical records, folklore and oral traditions, and revenue documents. Material remains — monuments, excavated sites, artefacts, sculptures and paintings — are archaeological sources, and their analysis often involves laboratory testing.

A word to know
Epigraphic source — texts, decrees or records inscribed on durable materials such as stone, metal plates or rock surfaces. Numismatic source — coins, currency or medals, which tell historians about the economy, chronology, rulers, trade and political boundaries through their metal content, inscriptions and symbols. Genealogical records trace family lineage, recording births, marriages and deaths.

Who is in it

Political Science is the study of governance, which informs us how and why power is distributed, decisions are made, and policies are implemented. It studies constitutions, governments and institutions of the State, as well as social movements, nation building, foreign policy, and the ways power is exercised, shared and regulated in society and everyday life.

In India's villages, the Panchayati Raj system embodies grassroots democracy by giving citizens a voice in local development planning. This shows that political power exists not only within formal institutions but also in social relationships, customs and ideas of legitimacy. To study politics, therefore, is to examine society itself — its hierarchies and its struggles for more effective and accountable governance.

Threads of curiosity
The study of politics in India began early, and was not treated as a separate discipline: it was linked to dharma (moral duty), artha (economic well-being) and rājadharma (the duties of the ruler). The Vedas, Upaniṣads and Purāṇas discuss justice, authority and social order; the Mahābhārata and Śhukranīti address governance, law and ethical leadership. Power was viewed as a responsibility rather than merely a privilege.
12Economics · keep it or sell it?Limited resources, and the choice that follows35 XP

One family, one harvest of 12 quintals of grain, and one decision. The family eats about a quintal a month, so every quintal carried to market is a month it cannot eat — and every quintal kept back is money it does not have.

Food in the house
—
Income earned
—
Verdict
—

Economics helps us understand how individuals and societies decide how to use limited resources to meet their needs. It studies how goods and services are produced, exchanged and distributed, and how these processes shape everyday life — from the food we eat and the clothes we wear to the jobs people do and the services they use.

It explores decision-making by consumers, producers and governments. Consumers decide what to buy, producers determine what and how much to produce, and governments frame policies to balance goals such as growth and stability, efficiency and fairness. In this way, economics is not only about numbers and markets but also about well-being, equity and justice.

Threads of curiosity
For centuries India was one of the world's leading economies and an important centre of trade, industry and maritime activity. Colonial rule disrupted this progress, causing widespread poverty, recurrent famines and the decline of traditional industries. Since independence the country has made significant progress in infrastructure, education and technology, poverty reduction and life expectancy — while the challenge of making growth reach every section of society remains.
Part 4 · Why any of this matters
13Why should we study Social Science?And what it is not for25 XP

After all the observing, questioning and evidence — how does this knowledge actually help you? Pick every reason the chapter gives.

The house you live in, the water you use, the roads you travel on, the school you attend, the markets you visit, and even the digital spaces you use are part of systems created and managed by society. You also live among people who may speak different languages, follow diverse customs and practise varied occupations. Social Science explains these variations as outcomes of geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors, and that understanding builds respect and cooperation — while helping us recognise how Indian culture binds this diversity together through an underlying unity.

In a democratic society, citizens play an active role in public life. When you understand how governments function and how decisions are made, you are better prepared to participate responsibly in civic life. Social Science is not about memorising dates, maps or definitions — it is about understanding people, places, society, culture and power.

Pause and ponder
The study of Social Science is a journey: from understanding how societies evolved, to analysing how they function today, to imagining how they can become better in the future. New technologies, expanding cities, environmental concerns, migration and global connections are reshaping how people live — and the skills you have practised in this chapter are the ones that make sense of them.
